question.text: Ms. Deepa Iyer, CIO of a large Indian corporate pension fund, is weighing whether to allocate 15% of her INR 5,000 crore corpus to alternative investments. Per NISM Ch 2.5 (Role of Alternative Investments in Portfolio Management), which of the following is the STRONGEST conceptual case she can make to her investment committee?

answer.text: Alternatives will guarantee higher absolute returns than traditional investments.

Alternatives provide risk diversification and access to off-market alpha sources; even when individual alts have higher standalone risk, held in a portfolio they can lower TOTAL portfolio risk via improved diversification.
Alternatives are cheaper in management fees than traditional mutual funds.
Alternatives are guaranteed by SEBI against capital loss.

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Chapter 2.5 and 2.6, the portfolio-theoretic case is that 'when held in a portfolio, these relatively high-risk investments could lower the total risk of the portfolio because of their ability to provide improved diversification', plus off-market alpha generation. Chapter 2.5 lists diversification, better risk-return trade-off, alpha from off-market strategies, and access to non-bankable growth companies as the four primary benefits. The Trap: Option A — guarantees are never valid in investment framing. Option B is false — alt fees (2/20) are far higher than MF fees. Option D is false — SEBI does not guarantee capital. Cross-Exam Context: XXI-B (PM) tests this via MPT/CML theory. XIX-A/B distributor tests it from suitability. XIX-C tests it from the manager's LP-pitch angle. Manager's Pro-Tip: When pitching a pension fund LP, anchor the diversification argument in correlation data — e.g., 'Indian Cat II private credit has 0.2 correlation to Nifty 50 over the last 7 vintages'. Round assertions about 'diversification' fail DD; correlation matrices pass.
